nameStory: The "highbush" part of this blueberry's name comes from its towering height compared to its lowbush cousins – it can grow 6-12 feet tall like a proper shrub rather than hugging the ground. The "northern" designation distinguishes it from southern highbush varieties, marking this as a true New England native that thrives in our cooler climate.
description: Northern highbush blueberry is a deciduous shrub that grows 6-12 feet tall, forming dense thickets in the wild or neat hedges in cultivation. It's the blueberry you're most likely to see in grocery stores, though wild ones have smaller, more intensely flavored berries. The shrub has an upright, branching growth habit with smooth-edged oval leaves that turn brilliant orange and red in fall. In late spring, it produces clusters of small, bell-shaped white or pink flowers that eventually become the familiar blue berries we all love.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The berries are the giveaway – dark blue with a powdery bloom (waxy coating) and a distinctive crown-shaped scar where the flower was attached. Wild berries are marble-sized while cultivated ones can be much larger. Taste one if you're certain of the ID – they're sweet-tart with tiny, barely noticeable seeds.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white or pinkish bell-shaped flowers hang in drooping clusters like tiny lanterns in late May and early June. Each flower is about 1/4 inch long and has a narrow opening – you'll often see bees working hard to squeeze inside for nectar.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves are 2-4 inches long with smooth edges (no teeth) and prominent parallel veins running from the midrib to the leaf edge. They feel slightly thick and leathery, and turn spectacular shades of orange, red, and purple in fall.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms upright shrubs 6-12 feet tall with multiple woody stems branching from the base. Wild plants often form colonies connected by underground runners, while individual shrubs have a vase-like shape with arching branches.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young twigs are green to reddish-brown and smooth, while older stems develop gray-brown bark that peels in thin strips. The bark has a slightly sweet smell when scratched – a family trait of the heath family.

habitat: Look for northern highbush blueberry in acidic, moist soils throughout New England – swamp edges, boggy areas, and the margins of ponds and streams are prime spots. It also thrives in partially shaded woodland clearings and along hiking trails where the soil stays consistently moist. You'll often find it growing alongside other acid-loving plants like mountain laurel, rhododendrons, and other members of the heath family.

seasonality.spring: White or pink bell-shaped flowers appear in drooping clusters in late May through early June, buzzing with bumblebees and other pollinators. New leaves emerge bright green and tender.
seasonality.summer: Green berries ripen to blue from July through August, with the powdery bloom becoming more pronounced as they mature. Leaves are dark green and fully developed.
seasonality.fall: This is when highbush blueberry really shines – leaves turn brilliant orange, red, and purple, making it one of New England's most spectacular fall displays. Berries may persist into early fall.
seasonality.winter: Bare woody stems show reddish-brown twigs and gray peeling bark on older branches. Flower buds are visible as small, plump, reddish bumps clustered at branch tips.

funFact: Blueberries are one of the only foods that are truly blue in nature – that distinctive color comes from anthocyanins, the same compounds that make them incredibly healthy antioxidants, and interestingly, a single blueberry bush can live and produce fruit for over 100 years.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with lowbush blueberry, but remember "high vs. low" – if you can walk under it, it's probably highbush! Lowbush blueberries rarely get above knee-high and have smaller, more tooth-edged leaves. Also distinguished from huckleberries by the berry's crown scar and soft seeds versus huckleberries' hard, crunchy seeds.
contextualKnowledge: What most people call "blueberries" in stores are typically cultivated varieties of this exact species – dozens of commercial cultivars have been developed since the early 1900s when blueberry cultivation began in earnest. Wild plants produce smaller but often more flavorful berries than their pampered garden cousins.
compareHints: Among its Vaccinium relatives, northern highbush blueberry is easily the tallest – lowbush blueberry stays under 2 feet, while lingonberry and the various cranberries are ground-hugging plants. The smooth-edged leaves help distinguish it from some other heath family members, and its upright shrub form separates it from the creeping cranberries that grow in true bogs.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its Vaccinium cousins, lingonberry is evergreen while blueberries lose their leaves in winter.
Differs from highbush blueberry mainly by size - lowbush stays under 2 feet while highbush can reach 6-12 feet tall.
American cranberry is much more robust than its cousin bog cranberry, with leaves twice the size and significantly larger berries.
Unlike lowbush blueberry which has green leaf undersides and toothed leaf edges, bog bilberry has distinctly pale leaf undersides and smooth-edged leaves.
Among New England blueberries, velvetleaf blueberry is the only one with distinctly fuzzy leaves - lowbush and highbush blueberries have smooth, hairless leaves.

Among its Vaccinium relatives, bog cranberry is distinguished by its extremely small size and creeping habit - while lowbush blueberries also stay low, they form upright clumps rather than trailing mats.
Unlike highbush blueberries that grow tall and upright, early lowbush stays under 3 feet and spreads horizontally.
Among New England's blueberries, black highbush stands out for its distinctively dark berries and fuzzy stems and leaves.
Unlike lowbush and highbush blueberries which have stamens that stay tucked inside their flowers, deerberry's stamens prominently stick out like tiny antennae.
Unlike its lowland cousins like lowbush blueberry and highbush blueberry, dwarf bilberry stays extremely small and produces single berries instead of clusters.
Compared to lowbush blueberry, northern blueberry prefers cooler climates and higher elevations, with slightly rounder leaves and often more intense berry flavor.
